newsitem.title: USA: Steady rates seen as Fed cites moderate U.S. growth.
newsitem.headline: Steady rates seen as Fed cites moderate U.S. growth.

text.p: The economy kept growing moderately in June and July, more vigorously in some regions than in others, but with little sign of rising wage and price pressures, the Federal Reserve said on Wednmesday.

The latest Beige Book summary of national activity, prepared by the Richmond, Va., Fed bank, said prices were being restrained by tough competition and wage pressures remained subdued despite increasingly tight labour markets.
Analysts said it meant the U.S. central bank was virtually certain to once again leave interest rates unchanged when its policysetting Federal Open Market Committee meets on Aug. 19.
The Fed last raised rates a quarter percentage point on March 25, citing strong demand as it acted to ward off potential inflation, and has kept them steady at two subsequent sessions.

"Economic activity generally expanded at a moderate rate in many districts in June and July, although several reported that growth was more brisk," the central bank said in its periodic summary of economic activity.
"Prices for most goods were stable, although reports indicated that lumber and some agricultural prices rose," said the Beige Book, so called because of its cover's colour.
Its findings were based on interviews with businessmen before July 28 in all 12 Fed districts.
"Clearly they were hearing just what they anticipated: moderate economic growth with little or no price pressures," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis.
"That means that at their next meeting on Aug. 19 the FOMC should not be doing anything because inflation continues to do very well and is in fact quite muted," Sohn added.
Investors appeared to be betting on the same outcome. Bond prices were steady after the closely watched Fed report was published while stock prices maintained a strong rally.

The Fed said overall prices were stable and were being held in check by "competitive pressures" in much of the country, though several regions said prices were rising for agricultural and energy products.
While labour markets continued to tighten, with shortages of employees from entry-level clerks to skilled computer operators, only "scattered" wage pressures were reported.
Sohn of Norwest pointed out that may change, however, citing the current strike by employees who are Teamsters' union members against United Parcel Service.

"It's all about money and pensions," he said, adding an eventual UPS settlement could become a model for later bargaining sessions between United Auto Workers' members and steelworkers and their employers.

In addition, the Fed report cited some constraints on output arising because of the lack of skilled employees. Aircraft companies in the San Francisco region said their production was being curtailed and the Chicago Fed said output in the Midwest was being curbed.
While consumer spending strengthened in the June-July period, automobile sales were "slightly softer," the Fed said.

"Manufacturing remained at a high level or expanded further across most industries, particularly for nonautomotive durables," the Fed added. However, most manufacturers said their inventories were at "generally desirable levels."
Raymond Worseck, economist for A.G. Edwards and Sons in St. Louis, Mo., said the overall picture was "steady as she goes" for the economy with no need for interest-rate rises soon to dampen activity.
"There is no significant change reflected in this report in what is really a benign outlook for inflation," Worseck said.
